Sort the error into a category before acting

A Claude Code error message usually tells you which category it belongs to, and the category decides your next move. The error reference groups messages into server errors, usage limits, authentication, network, request errors, command-line errors, plugin errors and tool errors. Deciding the category first keeps you from the most expensive mistake: retrying something that will never succeed, or rewriting a prompt to fix what was really an outage.
Error categories, a typical message in each, and what the category tells you
Category
Example message
What it tells you
Server errors
API Error: Repeated 529 Overloaded errors
Anthropic-side trouble; often transient
Usage limits
You've hit your session limit
Your quota or spend cap is used up; retrying won't help until it resets
Authentication
Not logged in · Please run /login
Credentials are missing or expired; the message names the fix
Network
Unable to connect to API
The path between you and the API is broken: connectivity, proxy or certificates
Request errors
Context limit reached · /compact or /clear to continue
The request itself has to change before it can succeed
Command-line errors
--bg and --print conflict
The way Claude Code was invoked is wrong; fix the flags
The HTTP status codes underneath follow the same split. A 529
means the API is temporarily overloaded. A 429
can mean a rate limit or a reached spend cap. A 400
means the request's format or content is wrong. If a failure persists and you need support, include the request ID from the error: every API response carries one.

What Claude Code retries for you, and what it won't
Predict first
Claude Code reports a 429 from your organization's gateway because a monthly spend limit was reached. What happens if you leave the session alone?
Claude Code retries twice, then reports the error
Nothing gets better: a spend-limit 429 isn't a throttle, so it isn't retried
Claude Code backs off and retries until the request goes through

Claude Code retries failures that are transient and that happen before any useful output exists. Server errors, overloaded responses and request timeouts that arrive before any of Claude's response has streamed are retried with backoff. So are dropped connections, including one broken because your computer went to sleep. Temporary 429 throttles are retried too. A message like
means this is already happening, and you should wait instead of intervening.
Some retries are deliberately capped:
Stalled stream:
a response stream that stalls before any response arrives is aborted and streamed again at most once.
Error after thinking:
a server error that arrives after Claude finishes thinking but before any text or tool call is retried up to two times.
Content filter:
a response stopped by the output content filter is re-sent once. A second block shows
Everything that needs a change from you stays failed. A spend-cap 429 has no retry-after header and keeps failing until access resumes. Authentication and request errors name their own fix, such as
or
. Waiting longer won't clear either kind.
Exam trap
Claude Code retries every 429, so a 429 always clears if you wait.
Why is that wrong?
Checkpoint 2 of 6
Check yourself
Your session shows an error and you're deciding whether to step in or let Claude Code handle it. Which of these situations will Claude Code recover from by itself if you just wait?
Your laptop went to sleep partway through a request and the connection dropped
"Not logged in · Please run /login"
"Output blocked by content filtering policy" appears after Claude Code has already re-sent the request once
"Context limit reached · /compact or /clear to continue"

Recovering from context pressure and autocompact thrashing
Compaction summarizes earlier conversation history to free room in the context window; the mechanics are in
Compaction (server-side and client-side SDK)

. Compaction can fail in a loop. If the context fills back to the limit straight after compacting, three times in a row, Claude Code stops with an "Autocompact is thrashing" error instead of burning more API calls. That error tells you something specific: whatever keeps refilling the window is still in the conversation, so compacting or retrying again won't help.
The fix is to stop the refill at its source. A typical case is reading a 40,000-line log in one go. Work through these steps in order:
Ask Claude to read the oversized file in smaller chunks, such as a specific line range or function.
Run
with a focus that drops the large output, for example
Move the large-file work to a subagent, so it runs in a separate context window.
Run
, but only if the earlier conversation is no longer needed.
Each step costs something different, so check what you are giving up. A focused
keeps only what you name, and anything else, like earlier hypotheses, survives only as summary.
drops the whole conversation, which is a poor trade in the middle of an investigation where the reasoning so far still matters. After recovering, check
. If Messages is the largest row, some output is refilling the window again. If the other rows together are larger, what loads at startup leaves too little room, so trim it.
can also return
even when the context is full, if a single large paste filled it.
Exam trap
Autocompact thrashing means compaction needs more attempts, so keep retrying until the large file fits.
Why is that wrong?
Checkpoint 3 of 6
Check yourself

Midway through an investigation, you ask Claude Code to read a 40,000-line service log in one go. The session then stops with "Autocompact is thrashing." You still need the reasoning built up so far. What should you do first?
Leave the session alone, because Claude Code will back off and retry the compaction by itself
Run /clear right away so the context window starts empty
Run /compact again a few times until the log fits after summarizing
Ask Claude to read the log in smaller chunks, such as a specific line range
Checkpoint 4 of 6
Exam question

During a long debugging session, Claude Code raises "Autocompact is thrashing: the context refilled to the limit..." immediately after automatic compaction completes, and it stops retrying. The team was asking Claude to read an entire 40,000-line production log file to find the root cause of an outage. What is the most effective way to recover and continue the investigation?
Raise CLAUDE_CODE_MAX_RETRIES so Claude Code keeps retrying compaction until the log file finishes loading successfully.
Ask Claude to read the log file in smaller chunks, such as a specific line range, or delegate the analysis to a subagent instead.
Set DISABLE_AUTO_COMPACT so Claude Code stops summarizing history and keeps the entire log output available for reference.
Run /clear to discard the conversation, then paste only the final error line from the log file into a fresh session.

Recovering a session that stalled on a refusal
A refusal blocks the conversation from the turn that triggered it. Why the model refuses is covered under
built-in safety classifiers and refusal fallback
. Recovering means getting back to a point before that turn. Press Esc twice or run
to return to a checkpoint before the triggering turn, then rephrase or take a different approach. If you can't tell which turn caused it,
starts a fresh conversation in the same project. The old conversation stays on disk and is still available in
Headless runs need a different path, because rewind isn't available under
. Retry with a rephrased prompt in a new session without
. Policy checks vary by model, so
can sometimes help as well. Sometimes the trigger is in a customization rather than your prompt. If the message shows
, look for an instruction telling Claude to write out its reasoning verbatim, which may sit in CLAUDE.md, a skill or an MCP tool description. To confirm, send the same prompt in a
session. After you change the customization, start a new session.
Checkpoint 5 of 6
Check yourself
A refusal arrives with "Details: [reasoning_extraction]". You suspect the trigger is a customization, not your prompt. Which step confirms that?
Send the same prompt in a claude --safe-mode session
Press Esc twice to rewind to before the turn, then send the same prompt again
Run /clear and send the same prompt in a fresh conversation in the same project
Rerun it headless with -p --continue so the same session retries the prompt

Finding the stuck or looping agent in a multi-agent session
When a multi-agent session stops making progress, first find which agent is stuck before deciding what to do. How spans and traces work is covered under
reading a trace: spans across a run and its subagents
. Claude Code tags each
OTEL span with
and

, and background subagent spans nest under the Agent tool span that dispatched them. Follow those IDs down the tree. The agent whose span stays open, or that keeps producing the same tool calls, is the one stuck or looping.
You can see the same tree without a tracing backend.

shows the nested subagent tree as work fans out, with a descendant count on each row and a path back to main. Runaway nesting has a ceiling: subagent chains are capped at five levels deep. Once you've found the stuck agent, press Ctrl+C to try to cancel the current operation. If the session doesn't respond, close the terminal and restart.
Apply it to your own work
The /agents tree shows one subagent whose descendant count keeps growing while the others have finished. What would you check in its spans before cancelling it?
Checkpoint 6 of 6
Check yourself

The /agents tree points to one subagent that keeps making the same tool calls. You press Ctrl+C to cancel the current operation, but the session stays frozen and doesn't respond to input. What is the next step?
Close the terminal and restart Claude Code
Press Esc twice to rewind to a checkpoint from before the subagent was dispatched
Leave it running, because Claude Code backs off and retries stalled work by itself
Run /compact so the looping subagent's output is summarized away
